abstract:
Non-fatiguing exercise modulates neural excitability in motor pathways controlling both exercised and unexercised muscles. Whether these effects also alter the synaptic control of spinal motoneurons remains unclear. This study investigated how acute non-fatiguing exercise influences motor unit discharge patterns and the estimated contributions of neuromodulatory input and excitation-inhibition balance, depending on muscle activation during exercise.

Fourteen participants completed two 30-minute rowing conditions involving either the upper body or the full body. High-density surface electromyography was used to assess tibialis anterior motor unit discharge properties before and up to one hour after exercise. The contributions of neuromodulatory input and excitation-inhibition balance to motor unit discharge were estimated using paired motor unit analysis and geometric characteristics of discharge patterns.

At matched torque, peak motor unit discharge rates increased following both exercise conditions, with effects persisting for up to 45 minutes. However, the estimated contributions of synaptic inputs differed between conditions. Following upper-body exercise, when the tibialis anterior was minimally activated, changes in motor unit discharge patterns suggested an enhanced contribution of neuromodulatory input, with no clear changes in excitation-inhibition balance. In contrast, the analyses following full-body exercise suggested a lower contribution of inhibition with respect to excitation, without clear evidence of enhanced neuromodulatory input. These findings suggest that similar increases in motor unit discharge rates following non-fatiguing exercise can be associated with different contributions of synaptic inputs.

Overall, our data suggest that acute non-fatiguing exercise induces sustained changes in motor unit discharge patterns, even in muscles minimally involved in the task. The estimated contributions of neuromodulatory input and excitation-inhibition balance to these changes appear to depend on muscle activation during exercise, providing new insights into the neural regulation of spinal motoneuron activity following non-fatiguing exercise.
